content.title: When will Artemis 2 reach the Moon? Where is Artemis II now? Check Artemis 2 tracker
content.text: When will Artemis 2 reach the Moon? Where is Artemis II now? Check Artemis 2 trackerGlobal DeskLast Updated: 01 April, 2026 08:41 PM -5 GMTSynopsisArtemis II tracker: NASA's Artemis 2 carries three Americans and one Canadian astronauts. Artemis II is the opening shot of NASA's grand plans for a permanent moon base.NASA's Artemis II crew of four begins historic mission to moon; Trump congratulates astronautsArtemis 2 tracker: The four astronauts aboard the Artemis II have reached orbit. They will circle the Earth for about 25 hours before catapulting toward the moon. Astronauts blasted off from Florida on Wednesday on NASA's Artemis II mission, a 10-day trip around the moon that would be the farthest humans have ever traveled and a major step toward returning people to the lunar surface this decade. The flight around the moon is humanity’s first lunar voyage in more than half a century and the leadoff in NASA’s push toward a lunar landing in two years.Astronauts on Artemis 2Carrying three Americans and one Canadian, the 32-storey rocket rose from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center where tens of thousands gathered to witness the dawn of this new era. Crowds also jammed the surrounding roads and beaches, reminiscent of the Apollo moonshots in the 1960s and ’70s. It is NASA’s biggest step yet toward establishing a permanent lunar presence.Five minutes into the flight, Commander Reid Wiseman saw the team’s target: “We have a beautiful moonrise, we’re headed right at it,” he said from the capsule. On board with him are pilot Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Canada's Jeremy Hansen. It was the most diverse lunar crew ever with the first woman, person of color and non-U. S. citizen riding in NASA’s new Orion capsule.How Long Will It Take Artemis 2 to Get to the Moon?Artemis II will hurtle several thousand miles beyond the moon, hang a U-turn and then come straight back. No circling around the moon, no stopping for a moonwalk — just a quick out-and-back lasting less than 10 days. NASA promises more boot prints in the gray lunar dust, but not before a couple practice missions.Artemis II is the opening shot of NASA's grand plans for a permanent moon base. The space program is aiming for a moon landing near the lunar south pole in 2028.The astronauts will stick close to home for the first 25 hours of their 10-day test flight, checking out the capsule in orbit around Earth before firing the main engine that will propel them to the moon.They won’t pause for a stopover or orbit the moon like Apollo 8’s first lunar visitors did so famously on Christmas Eve 1968, reading from Genesis. But they stand to become the most distant humans ever when their capsule zooms past the moon and continues another 4,000 miles (6,400 kilometers) beyond, before making a U-turn and tearing straight home to a splashdown in the Pacific.Once settled in a high orbit around Earth, the astronauts got ready to assume manual control and practice steering their capsule around the rocket’s detached upper stage, venturing within 33 feet (10 meters). NASA wants to know how Orion handles in case the self-flying feature fails and the pilots need to take control.Four days later during the lunar flyby, the moon will appear to be the size of a basketball held at arm’s length. The astronauts will take turns peering through Orion’s windows with cameras. If the lighting is right, they should see features never before viewed through human eyes. They’ll also catch snippets of a total solar eclipse, donning eclipse glasses as the moon briefly blocks the sun from their perspective and the corona is revealed.NEXT STORYBeyond the bling: How Indian wealth is repurposing itself in DubaiBeyond the bling: How Indian wealth is repurposing itself in DubaiET SpotlightLast Updated: 26 March, 2026 00:16 AM -5 GMTSynopsisIndian wealth is increasingly using Dubai as a long-term base for structured investing, governance, and global portfolio diversificationListen to this article in summarized formatET SpotlightReality TV enthusiasts will be familiar with Dubai Bling, the series that showcases the blingy, sometimes over-the-top lifestyle that the uber wealthy of Dubai enjoy. But when the teaser for Desi Bling, an Indian spin-off to the show, was launched in February, the sheer magnitude of Indian wealth and influence in Dubai came into the spotlight. Inside Dubai’s Cashless 2026 Shift Dubai’s Cashless 2026 Strategy, a government-led initiative that seeks to digitize 90% of all transactions across the emirate by the close of this year, signals more than a change in payment behaviour. It reflects a deeper shift in how businesses in Dubai are starting to move money, manage operations, and grow in a more digital system. This video explores what that means for enterprise payments, fintech growth, and business efficiency. As digital transactions become more deeply embedded, Dubai is not just changing how money moves; it is building the payments backbone of a more future-ready business city. Wealth migration to Dubai is not a new concept, but the pace and scale of Indian high-net-worth migration over the past decade has become increasingly significant. The number of High-Net-Worth Individuals (HNWIs) in the UAE has increased by 102% in the past decade. In 2024, 6700 HNWIs moved into the UAE and in 2025, the number was expected to be as high as 9800, according to Henley & Partners1.Trade agreements open markets. But what happens after determines who truly scales.As India–UAE trade expands under the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), the focus is shifting to execution, from tariffs to how efficiently goods move through ports and into global markets. This video looks at how Dubai is modernising customs, logistics infrastructure, distribution platforms, and payment connectivity.As monumental as this sounds, it is also linked with the reforms and global events that have triggered this shift in the past decade. Since 2016, the UAE has introduced business reforms, including 100% foreign ownership of businesses, bankruptcy law reforms, and easier access to long-term residency through the Golden Visa. The Golden Visa has opened up doors not just for the generationally wealthy, but also for high income earners and entrepreneurs. While zero income tax and inheritance tax may have held the initial appeal for HNWIs, global events have also triggered the exodus. The Covid-19 pandemic revealed the structural deficiencies in other markets. Where global lockdowns brought business to a standstill for months on end, the lockdown lasted a mere three months in Dubai, prompting individuals and businesses to relocate for its business continuity and effective health protocol management. Within this ecosystem, the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) has emerged as a critical anchor. An English Common Law Framework, robust regulation by the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA), secure and transparent environment with 100% foreign ownership of businesses, all of these have aided the credibility of the DIFC on an international scale so that wealth and businesses are moving from the UK, India, and Russia amongst others. This is evident in the growth of wealth and asset management entities by 22% in the past year2 alone. ET Spotlight One of the key areas of investment has been luxury real estate. Dubai has emerged as one of the strongest-performing luxury residential markets in the Middle East. According to The Wealth Report (2025) by Knight Frank, the value of luxury properties has risen by 147% in the past five years, reflecting sustained long-term appreciation.This momentum is reinforced by broader market activity: data released by the Dubai Media Office shows that overall real estate transactions in the emirate reached AED 431 billion in H1 2025. Within this landscape, market analysis from Savills indicates continued demand for homes priced above AED 10 million, particularly in established luxury districts such as Palm Jumeirah and Emirates Hills, where limited supply has supported price stability.Dr Bhaskar Dasgupta, Chairman of APEX Group, posits that real estate is increasingly being treated as a core part of HNWI portfolios and less as a ‘shiny purchase’. “Branded residences and fractional schemes are everywhere, but the trick is to stop thinking of property as an Instagram backdrop and start seeing it as a structured investment”, says Dr Dasgupta. For Indian investors, the capital flow is also supported by the positioning of such jurisdictions as GIFT City as the gateway for outbound allocation into markets such as Dubai, according to Dr Dasgupta. In this sense, Indian HNWIs are not simply leaving India for Dubai, they are establishing themselves across multiple bases for greater mobility. Generational shifts are also shaping how capital is deployed. According to Shelein Lakhani, Senior Wealth Advisor at Vault Wealth, younger members of wealthy families are increasingly open to alternative asset classes such as private credit and venture capital, particularly in sectors aligned with technology and sustainability.Dubai has emerged as a natural base for this shift. The emirate’s push towards economic diversification, coupled with the rapid growth of climate-tech, fintech, health-tech and AI ecosystems, has created a pipeline of opportunities that align with both commercial and social objectives. Family businesses are also increasingly allocating efforts to sustainable practices, such as Landmark Group’s Circulife, which recycles textile, spearheaded by the Jagtiani family. Another effort is Yusuff Ali family’s Lulu Group’s integration of solar energy into large warehouses and Reverse Vending Machines across retail operations reflect a broader shift towards responsible capital deployment.As wealth circulates through real estate and increasingly into regulated funds, innovation platforms, and sustainability-focused investments, Indian capital in Dubai is evolving beyond visibility and luxury. What is emerging instead is a more deliberate, long-term approach, one that positions Dubai as a stable base for governance, growth, and generational continuity.This article is authored by Amandeep Kaur Ahuja. The focus was not on models, chips, or cloud architecture, but on electricity.'AI and Electric Energy: Complementing for a Sustainable and Resilient Future', the official pre-summit in the run up to the India AI Impact Summit, was hosted by Hitachi Energy India and supported by the Ministry of Electronics & IT (MeitY). It gathered policymakers, diplomats, grid operators, and academics to confront a reality the AI boom has largely sidestepped: that every data centre is a factory, every query has a power footprint, and India's ambitions to become a global AI hub can be realised if the grid keeps pace. What will really power India’s AI boom?The AI conversation starts with electricity.In his keynote at ‘AI and Electric Energy: Complementing for a Sustainable and Resilient Future’ the official pre-summit to the India AI Impact Summit hosted by Hitachi Energy India (HEI) and supported by MeitY, HEI chief executive N Venu explored how energy will shape the next phase of AI in India.In this address, he explains: • How AI and energy intertwined • Why data centres must be treated like industrial assets • How grid reliability will define technological sovereignty • Why execution speed will determine leadershipWatch the full keynote to understand why India’s AI future will be decided as much in transmission corridors as it will be in code repositories.The framing was sharp from the outset. N Venu, MD and CEO, India and South Asia, Hitachi Energy, and MD of Hitachi India, put it plainly in his opening address: "Energy is both the ultimate enabler and the ultimate bottleneck." With global data centres projected to consume close to 1,000 TWh by 2030, AI is set to become one of the important new drivers of electricity demand within five years. For India, which is already navigating a massive renewable transition, this means rethinking how power systems are expanded and operated with grid stability.The pre-summit didn't waste time on whether India was ready. It assumed readiness was a given and moved straight to execution. MeitY Secretary S Krishnan laid out the sequencing: "You start with power, then build compute, then models, and finally data. Without the foundational layer of reliable power, it is impossible to move to the next stage." His message to data centre developers was equally direct. "Data centres should not expect subsidised electricity. They must pay the full cost of power,” he underlined. India's pitch would rest on competitive tariffs, grid reliability, and speed of delivery, not handouts.That competitive advantage is real. RK Tyagi, Chairman and CMD, Power Grid Corporation of India, stated that "AI and data centres run on electrons. And in India, electrons are among the most affordable in the world." The country's visible data centre demand has doubled from around 8 GW to 16 GW, and the renewable target of 500 GW by 2030 signals serious infrastructure intent. He also emphasised that India has one of the most reliable transmission networks globally, making a case for the country as a data centre hub. The question is whether that capacity can beplanned, timed, and delivered to meet the specific demands AI workloads bring.And those demands are unusual. Ghanshyam Prasad, Chairperson of the Central Electricity Authority, dismantled the misconception that data centres do not behave like constant, predictable loads. He noted that "the AI use cases we see today are barely 1-2% of what will eventually emerge," pointing to the scale of transformation ahead. They require N+1 and N+2 redundancy, meaning utilities must plan for 1.4 to 1.5 times the stated capacity to guarantee uptime. They are globally-driven, volatile, and unforgiving of even brief interruptions.“Green data centres in India cannot rely on gas. Our pathway has to be predominantly renewable,” Prasad underlined. Traditional grid planning methods, built for industrial or residential demand curves, need to be redesigned for this.The plenary session also featured international perspective on this challenge. Jan Thesleff, Ambassador of Sweden to India, stated: “Nearly 95% of Sweden's energy comes from non-fossil sources: hydro, nuclear, and wind. Our data centres are powered accordingly. This is the result of marrying digital ambition with energy responsibility." He also added that in a fragmented global environment, partnerships on grids, decarbonisation, and open standards can be constants in uncertain times. Thesleff’s message was that technological leadership without energy sovereignty is incomplete.The panel discussion that followed pushed beyond megawatt counts to the unglamorous but essential details. Abhijit Abhyankar, Professor with the Department of Electrical Engineering at IIT Delhi, noted that about 40% of all data centre power is used for cooling. He also flagged water use, a constraint India cannot afford to ignore."Fifty AI prompts can consume about half a litre of fresh water… a 100 MW data centre may consume about two million litres of fresh water daily,” he said. Reliability choices carry carbon consequences too. Batteries help, but diesel backups remain the default, bringing emissions and logistics challenges. Abhyankar’s point was not to discourage development, but to plan honestly for what operations actually require.There was also a recognition that not all the burden has to sit on the grid. Abhishek Jain, Fellow and Director of Green Economy and Impact Innovations, Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), asserted that "moving away from generalised models toward fit-for-purpose use cases is a big unlock." Moving to fit-for-purpose, agentic systems can cut inference energy significantly. He also pointed out a key inefficiency: by the time AI models 'understand' what you want, they've consumed multiple queries worth of power. Shifting certain workloads from GPU-heavy stacks to CPU-based architectures and rapid chip design improvements can also reduce the energy cost per query. India's energy strategy, he suggested, should not assume a fixed power-per-prompt ratio. That number can move, and should.Vibha Dhawan, Director General, The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI), brought the focus to adaptability. She suggested decentralised possibilities such as building-integrated solar and village-level production, while stressing that efficiency gains can dramatically change the equation, just as solar efficiency improvements already have."You don't end up reinventing the broken wheel. You complete the wheel and start using it,” she pointed out. For data centres, this means making sustainability measurable through region-specific benchmarks, water recycling, and building design, not just headline capacity.BSES Rajdhani Power Limited (BRPL) CEO Abhishek Ranjan grounded the conversation in a basic prerequisite: data. "If you don't have metering across the power systems, you won't have the data needed for correct analysis,” he said. In essence, AI can optimise grids only if grids are instrumented. Metering, sensors, and hardware upgrades are the foundation for forecasting, dispatch, and reliability. Without visibility across the power systems, ‘AI for grid’ is a slogan rather than a tool. "Move from project-to-project approaches to programme-based approaches... do it once and replicate it 10 times,” he summed up.The pre-summit closed on a definition of energy security that went beyond generation and transmission. It included skills, training, test beds, and industry-academia bridges that carry ideas from early-stage research to real deployment. N Venu summed up the stakes clearly: "The choices we make and the collaborations we forge in rooms like this will determine whether India merely participates in the AI era or leads it."India can host AI at scale, but only if it treats AI load as a serious planning input, builds measurement and flexibility into the grid, and designs sustainability around real constraints like water and materials, not just capacity headlines. The pre-summit made the case that power infrastructure is not a footnote to India's AI story. It is the opening chapter.( Originally published on Mar 02, 2026 ) (This article is generated and published by ET Spotlight team. It also highlights the balancing act universities face between ensuring free expression and maintaining safety in unpredictable environments.NEXT STORYTax return postmark rules 2026: 1-day delay risk— Will mailing taxes last minute make your IRS filing late?Tax return postmark rules 2026: 1-day delay risk— Will mailing taxes last minute make your IRS filing late?By Piyush Shukla, Global DeskLast Updated: Apr 16, 2026, 06:00:00 AM ISTSynopsisA 1-day delay can now make your return late. The tax return postmark rules 2026 have changed how the IRS reads mailing dates. Many taxpayers still mail returns on April 15. But USPS now applies postmarks at processing centers, not at drop boxes. That means your envelope may get stamped on April 16. The IRS treats that as a late filing. Penalties and interest can start immediately. This shift is real and already affecting filers. The tax return postmark rules 2026 increase risk for last-minute mailing. Experts now advise early mailing or e-filing. Timing is no longer what you control. The system decides your official filing date now.Listen to this article in summarized formatIANSTax return postmark rules 2026: Why mailing your tax return last minute could now make it lateThe tax return postmark rules 2026 have quietly changed the risk of filing by mail, and the impact is immediate. Millions of taxpayers still rely on mailing their returns on deadline day, but new U.S. Postal Service processing updates mean that what used to be “on time” may now be considered late. That shift matters because the IRS continues to rely strictly on the postmark date, not the drop-off time. If your envelope gets stamped a day later, penalties can apply even if you acted before midnight. In 2026, this is no longer a hypothetical concern. Postal processing changes rolled out in late 2025 moved postmarking away from local collection points to centralized sorting facilities. That means a return dropped on April 15 may not be processed until April 16 or later. The result is a mismatch between taxpayer intent and official filing recognition. The tax return postmark rules 2026 now expose last-minute filers to late filing penalties, interest charges, and compliance risks. The answer to the main question is clear: yes, mailing your return at the last minute can now make it late under the updated tax return postmark rules 2026. The safest strategy has shifted toward early mailing, proof-based services, or digital filing. This is not just a procedural tweak. It is a structural change in how deadlines work in practice. And for taxpayers, it raises a simple but urgent question—can you still trust the mailbox on deadline day? What changed in tax return postmark rules 2026 and why it matters now The tax return postmark rules 2026 are shaped by operational changes inside the postal system, not the IRS itself. Previously, postmarks were often applied locally when mail entered the system. That created a close match between the time you mailed your return and the official filing date. Now, centralized processing has altered that timeline. Mail dropped into a collection box or even handed over at a counter may travel before receiving a postmark. That delay can push the official date beyond the filing deadline. As a result, the tax return postmark rules 2026 effectively disconnect mailing time from filing recognition. This matters because the IRS still enforces strict deadlines. If the postmark shows April 16 instead of April 15, the return is considered late. There is no adjustment for intent or effort. The system relies on documented timestamps, and under the tax return postmark rules 2026, those timestamps are now less predictable. Why mailing your tax return last minute is riskier under tax return postmark rules 2026 The biggest risk under the tax return postmark rules 2026 comes from timing uncertainty. Taxpayers often assume that mailing before the last pickup guarantees an on-time filing. That assumption no longer holds true. If you drop your return in the evening on deadline day, it may not enter processing until the next day. That delay shifts the postmark forward. The IRS sees only the stamped date, not the drop-off moment. Under the tax return postmark rules 2026, this creates a gap where compliant behavior can still lead to penalties. Late filing penalties can reach 5 percent per month of unpaid taxes, with additional interest accumulating daily. Even a short delay can trigger costs. This makes last-minute mailing a high-risk strategy. The tax return postmark rules 2026 effectively penalize reliance on timing assumptions that no longer reflect how the system operates.How to safely file your return under tax return postmark rules 2026 Adapting to the tax return postmark rules 2026 requires a shift in filing habits. The most reliable approach is early action. Mailing your return several days before the deadline reduces exposure to processing delays and ensures timely postmarking. If mailing on the final day is unavoidable, visiting a post office counter and requesting a hand-stamped postmark can provide more control. This reduces reliance on automated sorting timelines. However, even this method depends on staff handling and timing, so it is not entirely risk-free under the tax return postmark rules 2026. Electronic filing remains the most secure option. It provides an instant timestamp recognized by the IRS. There is no dependency on physical handling or postal workflows. In the context of the tax return postmark rules 2026, e-filing eliminates the uncertainty that now defines last-minute mailing.Tax return postmark rules 2026 FAQs: What taxpayers are now searching and asking Many taxpayers are asking whether the IRS changed its rules. The answer is no. The IRS still follows the same legal framework. The shift comes from how mail is processed. The tax return postmark rules 2026 reflect operational changes, not regulatory ones. Another common question is whether certified mail protects against delays. It helps by providing proof of mailing, but it does not override the postmark requirement. The IRS still relies on the stamped date. Under the tax return postmark rules 2026, documentation supports your case but does not guarantee compliance. Taxpayers also ask if extensions are safer. Filing for an extension electronically ensures you meet the deadline for requesting more time. However, any taxes owed must still be paid on time. The tax return postmark rules 2026 do not change payment obligations, only the risks tied to mailing. Finally, many wonder if this change is temporary. Current indications suggest it is not. Centralized processing is now a core part of postal operations. That means the tax return postmark rules 2026 will likely remain relevant in future tax seasons. The tax return postmark rules 2026 redefine what “filing on time” looks like for mailed returns. The system no longer aligns neatly with taxpayer behavior. Instead, it depends on processing timelines that individuals cannot fully control. This shift demands a proactive approach. Mailing early, using verifiable services, or choosing digital filing are no longer optional strategies. They are essential safeguards. The tax return postmark rules 2026 highlight a broader truth about compliance in modern systems—timing is no longer just about action, but about verification. For taxpayers, the message is simple but critical. Do not rely on the last minute. Under the tax return postmark rules 2026, the margin for error has effectively disappeared.NEXT STORYJapanese proverb of the day, "A quiet river runs deep" - True strength does not announce itself loudly; it grows quietly within, steady, patient, and....Japanese proverb of the day, "A quiet river runs deep" - True strength does not announce itself loudly; it grows quietly within, steady, patient, and....By Piyush Shukla, Global DeskLast Updated: Apr 16, 2026, 06:21:00 AM ISTSynopsisJapanese proverb of the day: Over 70% of leaders now value emotional intelligence over loud confidence. It proves real power stays steady, hidden beneath the surface, yet deeply impactful and lasting.Listen to this article in summarized formatetimes.inJapanese proverb of the day a quiet river runs deep why data shows quiet strength drives leadership emotional intelligence and success todayJapanese proverb of the day: In a world driven by noise, speed, and constant visibility, the Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep” carries a striking truth backed by both psychology and real-world behavior patterns. Studies in behavioral science show that individuals who display calm, measured communication are often perceived as more competent and emotionally intelligent. This aligns directly with the deeper meaning of the Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep,” which suggests that true strength, wisdom, and resilience do not need loud expression. Instead, they grow silently, rooted in patience and inner stability.The Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep” answers a key modern question: does silence indicate weakness or strength? The answer is clear—quiet individuals often possess greater depth, focus, and emotional control. In today’s hyper-connected culture, where attention is currency, this proverb becomes even more relevant. It reminds us that not everything valuable is visible on the surface. Just like a deep river flows calmly while carrying immense power beneath, people with inner strength often move quietly yet influence profoundly.Japanese proverb of the day, "A quiet river runs deep" - True strength does not announce itself loudly; it grows quietly within, steady, patient, and deeply rooted beyond the surface.This timeless wisdom resonates strongly in American culture today, especially as conversations around mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and mental resilience gain traction. The Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep” is not just a poetic saying—it’s a philosophy of living with intention, patience, and depth in a fast-paced world that often rewards noise over substance.Understanding the Japanese proverb of the day: Meaning in modern lifeThe Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep” emphasizes that external silence does not reflect internal emptiness. Instead, it often signals depth, intelligence, and emotional maturity. In modern life, where social media amplifies voices constantly, quiet individuals can be overlooked. However, research suggests that introverted personalities frequently excel in critical thinking, decision-making, and long-term planning.This proverb teaches that strength does not require validation. A person who understands their value does not need to constantly prove it. The Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep” also highlights the importance of patience. Just as deep rivers flow steadily without turbulence, individuals with strong character remain composed even under pressure.Moreover, this proverb aligns with leadership trends in the United States, where quiet leadership styles are increasingly recognized. Leaders who listen more and speak less often build stronger teams. The Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep” therefore reflects a shift toward valuing depth over display, substance over noise, and consistency over chaos.The Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep” reflects true strength because it focuses on inner control rather than external dominance. Psychological studies show that people who regulate emotions effectively tend to achieve better outcomes in both personal and professional settings. This kind of strength is quiet, stable, and deeply rooted.Unlike loud confidence, which can sometimes mask insecurity, quiet confidence is built on self-awareness. The Japanese proverb of the day “A quiet river runs deep” suggests that individuals who do not seek attention often possess greater clarity of thought. They observe more, react less, and act with intention.In American workplaces, this idea is becoming increasingly relevant. Companies now value emotional intelligence as much as technical skills.
